procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
procedural_history.impugned_order: Common order dated 09.01.2024 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Petition Nos. 13095 of 2023 and 13153 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru issued a common order on 09.01.2024 in Criminal Petition Nos. 13095 of 2023 and 13153 of 2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant(s) approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court heard the appeals and ultimately allowed them.

directions: The impugned common order dated 09.01.2024 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Petition Nos.13095/2023 and 13153/2023 is set aside.

The orders dated 10.11.2023 passed by the Principal City Civil & Sessions Judge at Bangalore respectively in Criminal Appeal No. 1537/2023 and 1536/2023 stands quashed and set aside to the extent it put the condition to deposit of 20% of the fine amount payable under orders in CC Nos.13937/2023 and 13938/2013, passed by the Court of XXXVI Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bangalore City.

Restore the orders dated 10.11.2023 suspending the sentence of the appellant in both the cases, with the condition(s) imposed qua execution of bond and on such execution it will remain in force till the disposal of the above mentioned appeals pending before the First Appellate Court concerned.

issue.issue_text: Whether the signatory of a cheque authorized by the Company is a drawer and whether such a signatory could be directed to deposit any sum out of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial Court under Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (for short ‘NI Act’), as a condition for suspending the sentence in an appeal filed against his conviction under Section 138 of the NI Act?

facts: The appellant, an authorized signatory for a company, signed cheques that were subsequently dishonored.
The trial court convicted the appellant under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments (NI) Act.
In an appeal against the conviction, the appellate court suspended the sentence on the condition that the appellant deposit 20% of the fine/compensation amount, as per Section 148 of the NI Act.

The appellant challenged this condition, arguing that as a mere signatory for the company, they were not the 'drawer' of the cheque and therefore could not be subjected to the deposit requirement under Section 148.
law: Section 148 of the NI Act empowers an appellate court to direct the 'drawer' of a cheque, who is appealing a conviction under Section 138, to deposit a minimum of 20% of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial court.
The Court referred to a previous decision, *Shri Gurudatta Sugars Marketing Pvt. Ltd.*, which had interpreted the analogous Section 143A of the NI Act.

In that precedent, the Court held that for the purposes of Section 143A, an officer of a company who is merely an authorized signatory is not the 'drawer' of the cheque; the company itself is the drawer and holds the primary liability.
application: The Supreme Court found that Sections 143A and 148 of the NI Act are analogous, as both impose a financial liability specifically on the 'drawer' of the cheque, albeit at different stages of the legal proceedings (trial vs. appeal).

Applying the logic from the *Shri Gurudatta Sugars* case, the Court reasoned that if a signatory is not the 'drawer' for the purpose of paying interim compensation under Section 143A, they cannot be considered the 'drawer' for the purpose of depositing a portion of the fine under Section 148.
The Court held that merely being an authorized signatory for a company does not, by itself, make that person the 'drawer' of the cheque.

It concluded that the lower courts had applied Section 148 mechanically without considering the exceptional circumstance that the appellant was not the drawer. This fact should have exempted the appellant from the deposit requirement.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, holding that an authorized signatory of a company's cheque is not the 'drawer' for the purposes of Section 148 of the NI Act. Consequently, an appellate court cannot direct such a signatory to deposit a portion of the fine or compensation as a condition for suspending their sentence. The lower court's order imposing this condition was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the signatory of a cheque authorized by the Company is a drawer and whether such a signatory could be directed to deposit any sum out of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial Court under Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (for short ‘NI Act’), as a condition for suspending the sentence in an appeal filed against his conviction under Section 138 of the NI Act?
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, inferred from the context and the respondent's opposition, is that as an authorized signatory of a company's cheque, they are not the 'drawer' in their personal capacity. Therefore, they should not be directed to deposit a sum under Section 148 of the NI Act as a condition for suspending the sentence upon appeal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent resisted the appellant's contention and argued for the dismissal of the appeals.
The respondent argued that the legal precedent set in the 'Shri Gurudatta Sugars Marketing Pvt. Ltd.' case was inapplicable to the current case.
The respondent also argued that an authorized signatory is not the drawer of the cheque.

cases.case_name: Shri Gurudatta Sugars Marketing Pvt. Ltd. v. Prithviraj Sayajirao Deshmukh & Ors.
cases.principle: Merely because an officer of a company is the authorised signatory of a cheque, it does not by itself make him the 'drawer' of the cheque.

cases.case_name: Jamboo Bhandari v. Madhya Pradesh State Industrial Development Corporation Limited and Ors.
cases.principle: An Appellate Court, in an appeal against a conviction under Section 138 of the NI Act, cannot mechanically impose a condition to deposit an amount under Section 148(1) without considering whether the case falls within exceptional circumstances.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An authorised signatory who signs a cheque on behalf of a company is not the 'drawer' of the cheque for the purpose of determining penal liability; the drawer is the principal entity on whose account the cheque is drawn.
obiter: Penal statutes must be interpreted strictly, especially when determining vicarious liability.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An authorized signatory of a company's cheque is not the 'drawer' for the purposes of Section 148 of the NI Act. This status constitutes an 'exceptional circumstance' that exempts the signatory from the requirement to deposit a portion of the fine or compensation as a condition for suspending their sentence upon appeal. The lower courts erred by mechanically invoking the power under Section 148(1) without considering that the deposit requirement is intended for an appellant who is the actual 'drawer' of the cheque.
legal_tests_applied: Exceptional Circumstances Test: The court evaluated whether the appellant's status as a non-drawer signatory constituted an exceptional circumstance sufficient to exempt them from the deposit requirement under Section 148(1) of the NI Act.

Analogical Reasoning from Precedent: The court applied the legal principle established in a case concerning Section 143A of the NI Act (Shri Gurudatta Sugars), which held that an authorized signatory is not the drawer, to the analogous provision of Section 148 of the NI Act.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning opposes the mechanical application of statutory powers, particularly those imposing financial burdens, and instead requires a consideration of the specific facts and circumstances of the case.

It is an exceptional circumstance to require an appellant who is not the 'drawer' of the cheque to deposit a sum under Section 148(1), as that provision is primarily aimed at the appellant who is the drawer.
